title: Boolean logic in PLC programs
summary: AND, OR, NOT and XOR combine on/off signals. Almost every control function, from a lamp test to a safety interlock, is built from these four operations.

sections.heading: Signals as TRUE and FALSE
sections.body: A BOOL variable has exactly two values: **TRUE** (1, on) and **FALSE** (0, off). A pressed normally open button, a lit lamp and an energized coil are all TRUE. What a value *means* depends on the wiring: a normally closed stop button is TRUE while it is **not** pressed.

sections.heading: The four basic operations
sections.body:
| Operation | Structured Text | TRUE when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AND | `A AND B` | both A and B are TRUE |
| OR | `A OR B` | at least one is TRUE |
| NOT | `NOT A` | A is FALSE |
| XOR | `A XOR B` | exactly one is TRUE |

In Ladder Diagram, contacts in series form an AND, contacts in parallel form an OR and a normally closed contact symbol forms a NOT.

sections.heading: Reading a logic line
sections.body: `Motor := (Start OR Motor) AND Stop AND NOT Fault;` reads: the motor runs if Start is pressed **or** it is already running, **and** the stop circuit is healthy, **and** there is no fault. Brackets matter: without them AND binds stronger than OR, so `Start OR Motor AND Stop` would let Start bypass the stop circuit.

sections.heading: Truth tables and testing
sections.body: Write down every input combination and the expected output before testing. Two inputs give four combinations, three give eight. PLC Lab's practice exercises check such combinations automatically and report which case failed.
